Game options The following options can be selected or deselected prior to a game: Fountain If this option is activated, a well will be created on a random field on the game board before the start of the game. Tea tiles If this option is activated, there are 6 purple tea tiles in the game. If you take possession of the first purple palace, you receive 3 tea tiles. There are 3 merchants on the 1 tower tile, 2 merchants on the 2 tower tile and 1 merchant on the 3 tower tile. The player who wins such a tower tile first receives additional 1, 2 or 3 merchants. The year is 1822. After years of decay, it is time to rebuild the medina, located at the foot of the Atlas mountains. The architects and engineers of the city work to erect large and beautiful palaces and to renovate the damaged city wall. As the reconstruction of the old city progresses, the city's inhabitants flock through the alleys, and the contours of the new city gradually reappear!

Each turn, players must place two pieces on the board (except when allowed to skip this with a tea tile), either augmenting an existing building (or starting a new building if the current building of that color is finished), or expanding one of the other features of the city, like the market or the walls. Each player will claim one building of each of the four colors by the end of the game, giving one point per wooden piece attached to the building.

Also, if you own the largest building of a particular color you get a bonus for that color. Finally, there are bonuses for palaces around the well, as well as for the player who most recently connected one of their buildings to the walls, which grow from the four corners of the city.

Medina is a tense game by the great designer Stefan Dorra. This latest edition of the game features a double-sided game board (enabling a two-player game), almost 200 detailed wooden pieces, and updated gameplay, as well as rules and components never before published for this game!

See Medina for the original edition of this game.

[Rating: 3/10] The game was interesting, until it kept going on forever where people were making turns that couldn't benefit them, but benefited one other player. Terrible idea. Would be an easy fix though if there was some way the game could end early. But the end game for this ruins it for me.

[Rating: 3/10] As a lover of abstracts, I hated this game. Everything is a point, and building the palaces is a shitty exercise in push your luck. No thanks. Will never play again.

[Rating: 3.9/10] Plusieurs essais mais ce jeu ne me procure aucun plaisir. Certes, le matériel est original mais à l'utilisation, c'est barbant et redondant.

[Rating: 4/10] In this game everyone gets an even share of bricks in each of the four colors, and an even share of the neutral colored pieces and a set of four player colored claim markers. On your turn you place 2 of your pieces. Once a player uses one of their two placements to put down a claim marker on a contiguous blob of colored bricks, the structure can no longer be added to by any player and that player can no longer claim a structure of that color. [Rating: 4/10] It was well-hyped and respected by BGG, Tom Vasel liked it, and it looked so pretty.  And the components!  But the game REALLY fell flat for us.  It just has no direction.  The rules are theme are quite soulless.  This one is not for me, and was traded away.

[Rating: 4/10] This one is a nice looking but ultimately fairly bland area control type game. It feels quite dated and you are very limited on what you may actually do on a turn, a lot of placement is forced placement so some of the decision making is taken out of your hands. It is a shame because I wanted to like it, but I really really do not.  Sold in 2017.
